data.text:
I searched for each claim. Claims 0, 2 and 3 are supported. Claim 1 is supported only in a corrected form. I'm not quoting passages at length, so check the linked sources for the full wording.

**Claim 0: top of a loaded beam is in compression, bottom in tension. Supported as written.**
- The Illinois State Board of Education bridge unit says that in a beam bridge the beam's top surface "compresses," while the bottom edge stretches under "tension." Source: https://www.isbe.net/CTEDocuments/TEE-L610023.pdf
- Midas (a bridge-engineering software maker) says that when a load is applied to the bridge deck, the beams bend, causing compression at the top and tension at the bottom. Source: https://resource.midasuser.com/en/blog/bridge/understanding-beam-bridges-design-components-and-construction-methods
- A US patent describes the same pattern: the beam's own weight creates a downward deflection that creates tension in the lower flange and compressive forces in the upper flange. Source: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/8752225

**Claim 1: flood scour causes more than half of US bridge failures (about 53% in one study). Supported in a corrected form.**
- The 53% figure comes from Wardhana and Hadipriono (2003), who analysed US bridge failures from 1989 to 2000. A review citing the study says flood and scour, with the major 1993 flood disaster, contributed to the frequency peak of failures, almost 53% of all failures. Source: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237828707_Analysis_of_Recent_Bridge_Failures_in_the_United_States
- A ScienceDirect review describes the same study this way: an investigation of five hundred bridge failures between 1989 and 2000 across the US found 53% were due to flooding and scour related complications. Source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2214391221000386
- Other sources give different numbers. One paper puts flood/scour at 48 percent (https://www.hsaj.org/resources/uploads/2022/05/supplement.4.2.pdf). Wikipedia says it has been estimated that 60% of all bridge failures result from scour and other hydraulic-related causes. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_scour)
- The problems with the script:
  - The 53% covers "flood and scour" together, not scour alone.
  - It is "almost 53%", which is about half rather than clearly more than half.
  - It is a single 1989–2000 sample.
  - The 1993 flood inflated it.
- Corrected wording: "Floods and scour are the leading cause of US bridge failures. One study of failures from 1989 to 2000 put them at about 53%, and other estimates range from roughly 48% to 60%."

**Claim 2: riprap around a pier's foot is a standard scour defence. Supported as written, with a caveat.**
- A paper on riprap design says that to protect against scour, riprap has been the most commonly used pier scour countermeasure. Source: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/331806713_A_novel_method_for_riprap_design_of_scour_protection_at_bridge_piers
- A ScienceDirect review lists riprap, gabions, cable-tied blocks, and mattress systems among the bed-armouring countermeasures that have long been the most widely used. Source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2215098626000935
- The FHWA's HEC-23 guidance covers riprap at piers. The text I found is a Scribd copy: https://www.scribd.com/document/60354060/HEC-23-Countermeasures. The official FHWA publication is at https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/engineering/hydraulics/pubs/09111/09112.pdf. I did not read the FHWA page directly.
- Caveat: one review of riprap research highlights the deficiencies of riprap in arresting pier scour. (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225732566_Scour_and_scour_countermeasures_at_bridge_sites) So it is standard, but it has to be designed and sized properly.

**Claim 3: a 100 m steel span grows about 6 cm for a 50 °C rise (about 12 millionths per °C). Supported as written.**
- A physics reference gives steel at about 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C and lists bridges as a use. Source: https://physicsfundamentals.org/blog/thermal-expansion
- US bridge practice uses the same value in °F. The Idaho Transportation Department's bridge manual gives 0.0000065/°F for steel. Source: https://apps.itd.idaho.gov/apps/bridge/manual/14%20Joints%20and%20Bearings/A14.6%20Expansion%20Joint%20Design%20Procedure.pdf
- Chase Corp says according to AASHTO standards, the recommended coefficient of thermal expansion for steel girder bridges is 6.5x10−6 per °F. Source: https://blog.chasecorp.com/bridge-and-highway/cold-expansion-joints
- 6.5 × 10⁻⁶ per °F is about 11.7 × 10⁻⁶ per °C, which rounds to 12.
- My own calculation is ΔL = αLΔT = 12×10⁻⁶ × 100 m × 50 °C = 0.06 m, or 6 cm. The coefficient is the sourced part, and the arithmetic is mine.
